summary: BBN's host status report for December 20 to 30, 1971, noting that the Lincoln Labs TX2 became a server. It was updated by RFC 293.

plainLanguage.summary: A check on which network computers were awake over the holiday weeks.

subtitle: BBN's status report on which ARPANET hosts answered test connections from December 20 to 30, 1971.

tldr.problem: Users of the early network needed to know which hosts were working and available as servers.
tldr.mechanism: BBN tested hosts daily from its Terminal IMP by attempting an initial connection, and recorded each result as a one-letter code in a table, along with each host's status or prediction.
tldr.outcome: During the two weeks the Lincoln Labs TX2 (Network Address 112) became a server. The report updates RFC 287 and was itself updated by RFC 293.

today: RFC 288 is a historical host status report. It updates RFC 287 and is updated by RFC 293. Its status is listed as Unknown.

sections.title: What the Report Covers
sections.content: This RFC reports on the status of most network hosts from December 20 to December 30 (1971, per the RFC's January 1972 date). BBN celebrated Christmas and New Year's Day on December 24 and December 31, respectively. The report notes that the Lincoln Labs TX2 (Network Address 112) became a server during these two weeks.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a holiday-time report card for the network's computers.

sections.title: Hosts Left Out of Daily Testing
sections.content:
Some hosts were excluded from daily testing in two categories. The first is hosts not expected to function as servers (available to other sites) on a regular basis for at least two weeks: addresses 133 (BBN PDP-10 B), 15 (Case PDP-10) and 13 (Ames/Paoli ILLIAC/B6500).

The second is hosts intended to be users only. These include the Terminal IMPs then on the network (AMES, MITRE, NBS and BBN), the Network Control Center computer (address 5), which only gathers statistics, and the Rand IBM-360/65, Harvard PDP-1, Illinois PDP-11 and NBS PDP-11. The BBN Terminal IMP (address 158) is a prototype that is often disconnected while its programs are refined and debugged.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers were not tested because they only visit other computers and never serve anyone, or were not expected to be ready.

sections.title: The Status Tables and Codes
sections.content:
One table lists each host's address, site, computer, status or prediction (such as Server, SOON, User only, or a month), and who supplied the prediction. Two more tables give the test result for each host on each test date, using the one-letter codes in the legend. A hash mark before a result means the site advertised that its system might not be available then.

A host counted as timed out (T) if it did not complete the ICP and open a connection within 60 seconds. The UCLA IBM-360/91 offered only a Network Job Service (NETRJS), which the BBN Terminal IMP could not test, so a successful initial connection to the NETRJS logger was assumed to mean NETRJS was working.
sections.plainLanguage: Each computer gets a letter for each day: open, dead, half-open, refused or too slow.

items.label: Dead
items.desc: Host dead or inaccessible from the BBN Terminal IMP.

items.label: 1/2 Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection, then closed it or stopped responding.

items.label: Open
items.desc: Host opened a connection and was accessible to users.

items.label: Refused
items.desc: Host returned a CLS to the initial RFC.

items.label: Timed out
items.desc: Host did not complete the ICP and open a connection within 60 seconds.
